First Chapter: The Discourse on Brahmā’s Entreaty (Brahmāyācanasutta)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“This Dhamma that I have realized is profound, hard to see, difficult to awaken to, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.
Yet this generation delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment.
For a generation that delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment, this state is difficult to see: namely, specific conditionality and dependent origination.”
"This state, too, is difficult to see: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others did not understand me, that would be weariness for me, that would be a vexation for me.
Then these verses, never heard before, occurred to the Blessed One: [The verses follow.]
“It was attained by me with difficulty;
enough now with proclaiming it!
For those overcome by lust and hatred,”
This Dhamma is not easily awakened to;
it goes against the stream, is subtle,
profound, difficult to see, and minute.
“Those who are stained by passion do not see,
being shrouded by a mass of darkness.
Thus, as the Blessed One reflected, his mind inclined toward inaction rather than toward teaching the Dhamma.
Then, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind, it occurred to the Brahmā Sahampati:

“Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is being destroyed! For the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines his mind toward inaction rather than toward teaching the Dhamma.”
Then Brahmā Sahampati—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—disappeared from the Brahma-world and reappeared before the Blessed One.
Then Brahmā Sahampati arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed him thus:
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Sugata teach the Dhamma!"
“There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, through not hearing the Dhamma, are falling away;
there will be those who understand the Dhamma.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said. Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“In the past, an impure Dhamma appeared among the Magadhans, conceived by those still stained with defilements.
Open this door to the Deathless!”
Listen to the Dhamma realized by the Stainless One.
Just as one standing on the peak of a mountain might see the people all around, so too [does he see].
Having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, O wise one,
with eyes all-seeing and free from sorrow, look upon the people overwhelmed by grief.
Behold those overcome by birth and old age!
Arise, O Hero, victor in battle;
O Caravan-Leader, free from debt, wander through the world!
"May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma;
there will be those who understand.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the Brahmā’s entreaty and out of compassion for beings, surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.
As the Blessed One surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha, he saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes,
with keen faculties and with dull faculties, of good disposition and of bad disposition, easy to instruct and difficult to instruct;
some dwelling perceiving the fear of blame regarding the world beyond, and others dwelling not perceiving the fear of blame regarding the world beyond.
Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses— some of those blue, pink,
or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and, not having risen above the water,
thrive submerged within it; while some of those blue, pink, or white lotuses are born in the water and grow in the water...
They have grown to the same level as the water; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand rising above the water, unsullied by the water.
In the very same way, the Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes.
Seeing that some possessed keen faculties and some dull faculties, some were of good disposition and some of bad disposition, some were easy to instruct and some difficult to instruct,
and that some dwelt perceiving the fear of blame and the next world while others dwelt without perceiving the fear of blame and the next world,
Brahmā Sahampati replied to him with a verse:
“The doors to the Deathless are opened for those who have ears;
let them release their faith.
Perceiving harm, I did not speak what is beneficial.”
“The sublime Dhamma among humans, O Brahmā.

Then Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, “I have been granted permission by the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma,” paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 6.2* (SN 6.2, SN 173, PTS [1st ed. SN i 138; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 303)
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on Reverence.
Thus have I heard—
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having just attained full enlightenment.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“It is indeed painful to dwell without respect and without deference. What ascetic or brahmin might I honor, revere, and rely upon as I dwell?”
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"For the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue that is not yet fulfilled, I might dwell depending upon, honoring, and revering another ascetic or brahmin.
Yet, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, I do not see anyone—"
In this world with its devas and humans, there is no other ascetic or brahmin more perfected in virtue than myself,
whom I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon.
For the sake of fulfilling the aggregate of concentration that is as yet incomplete, I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon another ascetic or brahmin.
Yet, in this world with its devas... I do not see another ascetic or brahmin more perfected in concentration than myself, whom I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon.
For the fulfillment of the aggregate of wisdom that is as yet incomplete, I would honor, revere, and live in dependence upon another ascetic or brahmin.

Moreover, I do not see any other ascetic or brahmin, whether among the devas... [or in this world], who is more accomplished in wisdom than myself, whom I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon.
It is only for the sake of fulfilling the aggregate of liberation that is as yet incomplete that I would honor, revere, and live in dependence upon another ascetic or brahmin.

Yet, I do not see any other ascetic or brahmin, whether among the devas... [or] more accomplished than myself in the perfection of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, whom I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon.
However, for the sake of fulfilling the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation that is as yet incomplete, I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon another ascetic or brahmin.
But, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins... [who could fulfill it].
"In this world with its devas and humans, there is no other ascetic or brahmin more accomplished than myself in the knowledge and vision of liberation,
whom I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon.
What if I were to honor, revere, and live in dependence upon this very Dhamma that has been fully awakened to by me?"
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
disappeared from the Brahma-world and reappeared before the Blessed One.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
"It is so, Blessed One; it is so, Sugata.
Those who were the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, in the past, those Blessed Ones also dwelt honoring, respecting, and relying upon the Dhamma alone."
"Venerable sir, those who will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future time—those Blessed Ones too, having honored and revered the Dhamma alone, will dwell depending upon it.
May the Blessed One too, venerable sir, who is now an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell honoring and revering the Dhamma alone, depending upon it.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said. Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“Those who were the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past,
those Buddhas who are yet to come,
and he who is the Perfectly Awakened One now— ”
The destroyer of the sorrow of many.
All those who revere the true Dhamma have lived and still live [in this way].
Nevertheless, they will continue to dwell [thus];
this is the natural law of the Buddhas.
Therefore, by one who desires their own welfare,
By one desiring the highest state,
the true Dhamma should be held in reverence,
remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 6.3 (SN 6.3, SN 174, PTS [1st ed. SN i 140, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 306) 1. First Chapter: Brahmadeva Sutta At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean, and there was a blind turtle that would surface once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, eventually insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole? “It would be so, venerable sir. After a very long time, it might happen that the blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, would insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole. “I tell you, bhikkhus, that it is not easy for that blind turtle to insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole even after a very long time; yet, bhikkhus, it is more difficult still to obtain the human state. And when one has obtained the human state, bhikkhus, it is not easy to obtain birth in a noble family. And when one has obtained birth in a noble family, bhikkhus, it is not easy to obtain the arising of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And when the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One has arisen, bhikkhus, it is not easy to hear the Dhamma. And when the right path has been attained, bhikkhus, it is not easy to attain the right view. And when the right view has been attained, bhikkhus, it is not easy to attain the right concentration. And when the right concentration has been attained, bhikkhus, it is not easy to attain the destruction of the taints. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin woman had a son named Brahmadeva who had gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Brahmadeva, in no long time,

realized for himself through direct knowledge and attained in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He dwelt having reached it.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the venerable Brahmadeva became one of the arahants.
Then, in the morning, the venerable Brahmadeva dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
While walking for alms from house to house in Sāvatthī, he approached the residence of his own mother.
Now at that time, the brahmin lady who was the venerable Brahmadeva’s mother was constantly offering oblations to Brahmā.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Sahampati:
“This mother of the venerable Brahmadeva, the brahmin lady, constantly offers oblations to Brahmā.
Suppose I were to approach her and inspire a sense of spiritual urgency in her.
Then, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, Brahmā Sahampati [vanished from that place].
Just as one might extend an arm that had been drawn in, or draw it in again after extending it, even so, having vanished from the Brahma-world,
he reappeared in the dwelling of the venerable Brahmadeva’s mother.
Then, standing in the air, Brahmā Sahampati addressed the brahmin lady, the mother of the venerable Brahmadeva, with a verse:
“Far from here, O Brahmin woman, is the Brahma-world,
for which you constantly offer oblations;
such as this is not the eater of Brahma, O Brahmin woman.”
Why do you mutter the path of Brahmā, not knowing it?
For this Brahmadeva of yours, O brahmin woman,
is one who is free from substrate and has surpassed even the gods.
The monk who possesses nothing, who does not support others,
he who has entered the house for alms— such a one is worthy of offerings,
a knower of the Vedas, one whose self is cultivated.
Worthy of offerings from both humans and gods,
having warded off evils and remaining unsmeared by them,
he wanders for alms, having become cooled.
For him there is neither past nor future;
he is peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and without longing;
he has laid down the rod toward all beings, both those who tremble and those that are stable.
Therefore, let him consume this offering, this foremost portion.
Free from enmity, with a peaceful mind,
he wanders unshakable like a tamed elephant.
Let that bhikkhu of virtuous conduct and well-liberated mind enjoy this offering, this foremost alms-food.
Those who have faith in him, being unshakable, [should offer it].
Establish the offering upon those worthy of offerings;
perform merit for the sake of future happiness,
O brahmin woman, having seen the Sage who has crossed over the flood.
Full of faith and unshakable toward him,
she established an offering for one worthy of offerings;
she performed a merit that brings future happiness.
Seeing the Sage who had crossed the flood, the brahmin woman [spoke].
Saṁyutta Nikāya 6.4 (SN 6.4, SN 175, PTS (1st ed. SN i 142, PTS (2nd ed. SN i 310) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga)
The Discourse to Baka the Brahmā.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, such an evil speculative view had arisen in Baka the Brahmā:
"This is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal, this is absolute, this is subject to no decay;
for this is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear; and there is no other escape higher than this."
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the Brahmā Baka—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
disappeared from Jeta’s Grove and reappeared in that Brahma-world.
Baka Brahmā saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Come, dear sir! Welcome to you, dear sir!"
"It has been long indeed, dear sir, since you made this occasion for coming here.
For this, dear sir, is permanent; this is stable; this is eternal; this is absolute;
this is subject neither to passing away nor to rebirth. And beyond this, there is nothing further."
“There is no escape.
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Baka Brahmā:
“Baka Brahmā is indeed immersed in ignorance; Baka Brahmā is indeed immersed in ignorance!”
For here indeed, while it is truly impermanent, he will say it is permanent; while it is truly unstable, he will say it is stable;
while it is truly non-eternal, he will say it is eternal; while it is truly incomplete, he will say it is complete;
and while it is truly subject to falling away, he will say it is not subject to falling away.
And where there is birth, aging, death, passing away, and rebirth, he will describe that thus:
"For this is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not undergo rebirth.
And though there is another, higher escape, he will say: "There is no other higher escape."
“Seventy-two were the meritorious deeds of Gotama,
by which he became a master of power and transcended birth and old age. This,
O Knower of the Vedas, is his final rebirth in the Brahma-world.”
“Many people are chanting for us.
“For this is but little, Baka, not a long life, though you consider it a long life.”
“O Brahmā, I know your lifespan to be one hundred thousand nirabbudas.
“I am the Blessed One of infinite vision.”
Having transcended birth, old age, and sorrow,
tell me what my former vows and virtuous conduct were, so that I may understand them.
“That which you caused many people to drink when they were thirsty, exhausted by the heat—
that was your former practice of vows and virtuous conduct.”
Just as one awakened from sleep, I remember:
how, at Eṇikūla, I liberated the people who had been seized and were being led away as captives.
I remember that ancient practice of yours, your conduct and observances,
just as one who has woken from sleep remembers a dream.
You were seized by the current of the Ganges while aboard your boat.
By force and by overcoming him, you liberated the Naga Ludda who desired to become a human;
that is your ancient practice of vows and virtuous conduct.
Just as one awakened from sleep, I remember:
for an eon I was your attendant, yet I did not honor you,
who possessed perfect enlightenment and were a speaker of truth.
“I remember that ancient practice of yours,
like one awakened from sleep.
“Surely you understand this lifespan of mine;”
"You know others as well, for you are indeed a Buddha;
for thus does this blazing majesty of yours stand,
illuminating the Brahma-world."

Saṁyutta Nikāya 6.5 (SN 6.5, SN 176, PTS (1st ed. SN i 144, PTS (2nd ed. SN i 314) 1. First Chapter: A Certain Brahmā Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then a certain Brahmā, having approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him and stood to one side. Standing there, that Brahmā said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless. Venerable sir, does the Blessed One declare this? “I do not say so, Brahmā. “Then, venerable sir, it is said, ‘The world is not eternal; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless. Venerable sir, does the Blessed One declare this? “I do not say so, Brahmā. [In the same manner, the Brahmā asks and the Blessed One replies negatively regarding the following views: “The world is finite... infinite... the soul and the body are the same... the soul is one thing and the body another... after death a Tathāgata exists... after death a Tathāgata does not exist... after death a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist... after death a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless. “I do not say so, Brahmā. “But, venerable sir, since the Blessed One does not declare any of these things, is it because the Blessed One does not know them? “I know, Brahmā, and I see that the world is finite, yet I do not declare it. I know, Brahmā, and I see that the world is infinite, yet I do not declare it. ... [and so on for all the other views]. “Why is that, venerable sir? Because, Brahmā, these doctrines are unbeneficial, irrelevant to the fundamentals of the holy life, and do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna. Therefore, I do not declare them. “But what, venerable sir, does the Blessed One declare? “I teach, Brahmā, the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with the eye, for its fading away and cessation. I teach the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind, for its fading away and cessation. This, Brahmā, is what I declare. When this was said, that Brahmā said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, what is that Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is that Dhamma which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, what is that Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure? It is this Fourfold Foundation of Mindfulness; that is, the contemplation of the body in the body, feelings in feelings, mind in mind, and phenomena in phenomena. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, what is that Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure? It is this Threefold Training; that is, training in higher virtue, training in higher mind, and training in higher wisdom. This, bhikkhus, is that Dhamma which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. The setting was Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin had developed such an evil view as this:
"There is no ascetic or brahmin who could come here."

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of that Brahmā—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—appeared in that Brahmā-world.
Then the Blessed One sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahmā, having entered the fire-element.
Thereupon, it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Where, indeed, is the Blessed One dwelling now?

Then, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw the Blessed One sitting cross-legged in the air above that Brahmā, having attained the fire-element.
Having seen him, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so did he vanish from Jeta’s Grove and reappear in that Brahmā world.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, leaning toward the eastern direction, sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahmā, having entered the fire-element attainment, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
"Where is the Blessed One dwelling at present?"
With his divine eye, the Venerable Mahākassapa saw the Blessed One...
Having seen him, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, even so did the Venerable Mahākassapa vanish from Jeta’s Grove and reappear in that Brahma-world.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, leaning toward the southern direction, sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahmā, having attained the fire-element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākappina:
“Where is the Blessed One dwelling at present?
With his divine eye, the Venerable Mahākappina saw the Blessed One … [and so on] … having entered the fire-element attainment.
Having seen him, just as a strong man might...
[as before] ...even so, vanishing from Jeta’s Grove, he reappeared in that Brahma-world.
Then the Venerable Mahākappina, leaning toward the western direction, sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahma, having attained the fire-element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Where is the Blessed One dwelling at present?
The Venerable Anuruddha saw him... [and so on] ...having entered the fire-element.
Having seen him, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his stretched arm, he vanished from that Brahma-world and appeared in the sky above that Brahmā,
sitting cross-legged in the northern direction, having attained the fire-element, yet remaining lower than the Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed that Brahmā with a verse:
“Friend, do you still hold that same view which you held before?
Do you see it passing away?”
“Radiant in the Brahma-world.
“My dear sir, that view which I formerly held is no longer my view.”
I see one shining forth in the Brahma-world, having transcended [all bonds];
how then could I speak ill of him today?
“I am permanent, I am eternal.
Then the Blessed One, having inspired a sense of urgency in that Brahmā,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, vanished from that Brahmā-world and reappeared right there in Jeta’s Grove.
He appeared in the Jeta Grove.
Then that Brahmā addressed a certain member of his assembly:
"Come, dear sir, go to where the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is; having approached him, speak thus to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:"

“Venerable Moggallāna, are there indeed other disciples of that Blessed One who possess such great psychic power and such great majesty, just as you, venerable Moggallāna, and Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha?
“Yes, sir,” that member of Brahmā’s retinue replied to that Brahmā. Having responded, he approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Venerable Moggallāna, are there other disciples of that Blessed One who possess such great supernormal power and such great majesty,
just as you, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha do?
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed that member of Brahmā’s retinue with a verse:
“Possessing the threefold knowledge, attained to supernormal powers,
skilled in the penetration of others' minds,
they are Arahants with taints destroyed.”
“There are many disciples of the Buddha.
Then that member of Brahmā’s assembly, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s words, approached that Brahmā and said to him:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna has spoken thus:”
Possessors of the threefold knowledge, attained to supernormal powers,
skilled in the ways of others' minds,
they are Arahants whose taints are exhausted.
“There are many disciples of the Buddha.
This is what that member of Brahmā’s retinue said.
And that Brahmā, being satisfied, rejoiced in the words of that member of Brahmā’s retinue.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 6.6 (SN 6.6, SN 177, PTS [1st ed. SN i 146, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 318) 1. First Chapter: Brahmaloka Sutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five lower fetters. What five? They are: identity view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust, and ill will. These, bhikkhus, are the five lower fetters. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these five lower fetters? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these five lower fetters has, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, become one of spontaneous birth, due to attain Nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these five higher fetters? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these five higher fetters has, with the utter destruction of the five higher fetters, become one of non-returning, due to attain Nibbāna there without ever returning to this world. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these five lower fetters and from the five higher fetters? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters has, with the utter destruction of the taints, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters and from the taints? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters and from the taints has, with the utter destruction of the taints, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters and from the taints. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, and from the aggregates? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, and from the aggregates has, with the utter destruction of attachment, hatred, and delusion, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, and from the aggregates. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, and from all suffering? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, and from all suffering has, with the utter destruction of attachment, hatred, and delusion, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, and from all suffering. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, and from the world? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, and from the world has, with the utter destruction of attachment, hatred, and delusion, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, and from the world. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, and from all formations? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, and from all formations has, with the utter destruction of attachment, hatred, and delusion, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, and from all formations. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, and from all consciousness?

“Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, and from all consciousness has, with the utter destruction of attachment, hatred, and delusion, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, and from all consciousness. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, from all consciousness, and from all perception? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, from all consciousness, and from all perception has, with the utter destruction of attachment, hatred, and delusion, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, from all consciousness, and from all perception. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, from all consciousness, from all perception, and from all contact? “Bhikkhu, one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, from all consciousness, from all perception, and from all contact has, with the utter destruction of attachment, hatred, and delusion, entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is the destination, this is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, from all consciousness, from all perception, and from all contact. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the final goal for one who is liberated from these ten fetters, from the taints, from the aggregates, from all suffering, from the world, from all formations, from all consciousness, from all perception, from all contact, and from all feeling?”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had retired for his midday rest in seclusion.
Then Subrahmā the independent Brahmā and Suddhāvāsa the independent Brahmā approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they stood leaning against the respective doorposts. Then the independent Brahmā Subrahmā said this to the independent Brahmā Suddhāvāsa:
"It is not yet the right time, dear sir, to attend upon the Blessed One."
"The Blessed One has gone for his midday rest and is in seclusion.
Yet that certain Brahma-world is prosperous and flourishing, yet there the Brahma dwells in negligence.
Come, dear sir, let us go to that Brahma-world; having approached, we shall cause that Brahma to be stirred."
“Even so, dear sir,” the independent Brahmā Suddhāvāsa replied to the independent Brahmā Subrahmā.

Then the independent Brahmā Subrahmā and the independent Brahmā Suddhāvāsa—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—in the same way, vanished from before the Blessed One and reappeared in that Brahma-world.
That Brahmā saw those Brahmās coming from afar. Having seen them, he said this to those Brahmās:
“Now then, dear sirs, where have you come from?
“We have come, dear sir, from the presence of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
But would you, dear sir, go into the presence of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?”
When he had spoken thus, that Brahmā, not accepting those words, manifested himself a thousandfold and said this to Subrahmā the Independent Brahmā:
“Do you not see, dear sir, such power and majesty of psychic potency as mine?
“I do indeed see, dear sir, such power and majesty of psychic potency as yours.”
“Thus, dear sir, being so powerful and so majestic, to what other ascetic or brahmin shall I go for attendance?
Then the paccekabrahmā Subrahmā, having manifested himself two thousand times, said this to that brahmā:
“Do you see such power and majesty as mine, dear sir?”
“I do indeed see such power and majesty in you, dear sir.
“But as for that, dear sir, the Blessed One is more powerful and more majestic than both you and I.
Go, dear sir, to attend upon that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
Then that Brahmā addressed the independent Brahmā Subrahmā in verse:
“Three *supaṇṇas*, four swans,
five hundred tigresses, and those who meditate;”
“O Brahmā, this celestial mansion of yours shines forth,
illuminating the northern quarter.
“Even though that mansion of yours shines thus,”
Illuminating the northern direction;
having seen the danger in forms, which are always trembling,
the wise one therefore does not delight in forms.
Then Subrahmā the independent Brahmā and Suddhāvāsa the independent Brahmā, having inspired that Brahmā with a sense of spiritual urgency, vanished right there.
And on a later occasion, that Brahmā came into the presence of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Then the Brahmā Turu approached the Blessed One and, having approached, stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Brahmā Turu said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many kinds of persons are there found existing in the world? “There are, Brahmā, three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which three? The person who is a worldling, the person who is a trainee, and the person who is one beyond training. These, Brahmā, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. “But, venerable sir, what is the distinction, what is the difference between these three persons? “Brahmā, the worldling is one who has not seen the Four Noble Truths as they really are. The trainee is one who has seen the Four Noble Truths as they really are, yet is still practicing for their full realization. The one beyond training is one who has fully realized the Four Noble Truths as they really are. This, Brahmā, is the distinction, this is the difference between these three persons. Trifling is this loss, that one loses wealth at dice; But the loss of all,
even including oneself, [is far greater].
This indeed is a much greater misfortune:
that one should harbor a mind of malice toward the Sugatas.
For a hundred thousand *nirabbuda* aeons, [one suffers].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 6.10 (SN 6.10, SN 181, PTS [1st ed. SN i 149, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 325) 1. First Chapter: The Discourse to Kokālika At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a blue lotus; the person who is like a red lotus; the person who is like a white lotus; and the person who is like a fragrant jasmine. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘like a blue lotus’? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. Just as a blue lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water—so too, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is ‘like a blue lotus. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘like a red lotus’? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. Just as a red lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, remains at the same level as the water and develops within it—so too, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is ‘like a red lotus. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘like a white lotus’? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. Just as a white lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands completely unsoiled by the water—so too, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is ‘like a white lotus. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘like a fragrant jasmine’? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. Just as a jasmine flower, though born on land and grown on land, does not rise up above the ground but rather emits its fragrance from the very earth—so too, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is ‘like a fragrant jasmine. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Kokāliya approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I do not see even a single bhikkhu among the Blessed One’s disciples who possesses such great supernormal power and might as the Venerable Sāriputta. “Kokāliya, do not speak thus! Do not speak thus! For the Venerable Sāriputta has great faith, great wisdom, great energy, and great mindfulness. But, Kokāliya, you yourself have little faith, little wisdom, little energy, and little mindfulness. Then the Venerable Kokāliya, being thus reproved by the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after he had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu Kokāliya has spoken out of ignorance; he has spoken what is contrary to fact. For the Venerable Sāriputta has great faith, great wisdom, great energy, and great mindfulness. But Kokāliya has little faith, little wisdom, little energy, and little mindfulness. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say of me: ‘The Blessed One is my teacher; I am a disciple of the Blessed One,’ and if they were to say: ‘The Venerable Sāriputta is my teacher; I am a disciple of the Venerable Sāriputta,’ then that person would be speaking what is true and not false. For, bhikkhus, the Venerable Sāriputta is wise, of great wisdom, possessed of the highest wisdom among the disciples of the Tathāgata. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the trees in the Himalayas, the Himavat, the Coral Tree is declared to be the foremost, so too, bhikkhus, among the disciples of the Tathāgata, the Venerable Sāriputta is declared to be the foremost in wisdom.

The Venerable Sāriputta is of great energy, of great ardor, of great perseverance, and of great fortitude among the disciples of the Tathāgata. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the trees in the Himalayas, the Himavat, the Sal-tree is declared to be the foremost, so too, bhikkhus, among the disciples of the Tathāgata, the Venerable Sāriputta is declared to be the foremost in energy. The Venerable Sāriputta is of great mindfulness, of great clear comprehension, of great self-possession, and of great composure among the disciples of the Tathāgata. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the trees in the Himalayas, the Himavat, the Great Sandalwood Tree is declared to be the foremost, so too, bhikkhus, among the disciples of the Tathāgata, the Venerable Sāriputta is declared to be the foremost in mindfulness and clear comprehension. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall be full of faith, full of wisdom, full of energy, and full of mindfulness. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves. When this was said, the Venerable Kokāliya spoke thus to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir! How well the Blessed One has explained the qualities of the Venerable Sāriputta! But, venerable sir, I do not see even a single bhikkhu among the Blessed One’s disciples who possesses such great supernormal power and might as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. “Kokāliya, do not speak thus! Do not speak thus! For the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna has great faith, great wisdom, great energy, and great mindfulness. But, Kokāliya, you yourself have little faith, little wisdom, little energy, and little mindfulness. Then the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires."
When this was said, the Blessed One said to the bhikkhu Kokālika:
“Do not speak thus, Kokālika; do not speak thus, Kokālika.
Set your mind at rest regarding Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are virtuous.”
A second time, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, although the Blessed One is trustworthy and reliable to me, nevertheless, venerable sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.
A second time, the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhu Kokālika:
“Do not speak thus, Kokālika; do not speak thus, Kokālika.
Set your mind at rest regarding Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are virtuous.
For a third time, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
“Even though... [as before] ...they have fallen under the power of their desires.
For a third time, the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhu Kokālika:
“Do not say so... [as before] ...”
“Sāriputta and Moggallāna are well-behaved.
Then the bhikkhu Kokālika rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Not long after the bhikkhu Kokālika had left, his entire body became covered with boils the size of mustard seeds.
Having been the size of mustard seeds, they became the size of mung beans; having been the size of mung beans, they became the size of kidney beans;
having been the size of kidney beans, they became the size of jujube stones; having been the size of jujube stones, they became the size of jujubes;
having been the size of jujubes, they became the size of myrobalans; having been the size of myrobalans, they became the size of beluva fruits.
They became the size of beluva-jujube fruits; having become the size of beluva-jujube fruits, they became the size of wood-apple fruits; having become the size of wood-apple fruits, they burst open.
Pus and blood flowed out.
Then the bhikkhu Kokālika passed away from that very affliction.
And having passed away, the monk Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Then, when the night had advanced, the Brahmā Sahampati—possessing a magnificent radiance that illuminated the entire Jeta Grove—approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.
He stood to one side. Standing there, the Brahmā Sahampati said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has passed away.
Having passed away, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has been reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna."
Thus spoke Brahmā Sahampati.
Having said this, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with his right side toward him, and vanished right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, last night, when the night was far advanced, Brahmā Sahampati—of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove—approached me.
Having approached, he paid homage to me and stood to one side.
Standing there to one side, monks, Brahmā Sahampati said this to me:”
“Bhante, the bhikkhu Kokālika has passed away.
Having passed away, Bhante, the bhikkhu Kokālika has been reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
This, monks, is what Brahmā Sahampati said; having said this, he paid homage to me, kept me on his right, and vanished right there.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu addressed the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, how long is the lifespan in the Paduma hell?
"The lifespan in the Paduma hell, bhikkhu, is indeed long."
"It is not easy to calculate it as 'this many years,' or 'this many hundreds of years,' or 'this many thousands of years,' or 'this many hundreds of thousands of years.
"But is it possible, Bhante, to provide a simile?"
“It is possible, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said.

“Suppose, bhikkhu, there were a Kosalan cartload of twenty measures of sesame seeds. If a man were to remove a single seed from it at the end of every hundred years, that Kosalan cartload of twenty measures of sesame seeds would more quickly be exhausted and come to an end by this method, than one *abbuda* hell would [be exhausted].”
Just as, monk, twenty Abbuda hells are equal to one Nirabbuda hell;
just as, monk, twenty Nirabbuda hells are equal to one Ababa hell;
just as, monk, twenty Ababa hells are equal to one Aṭaṭa hell.
Just as, monk, twenty Aṭaṭā hells are equal to one Ahaha hell;
just as, monk, twenty Ahaha hells are equal to one Kumuda hell;
just as, monk, twenty Kumuda hells are equal to one Sogandhika hell.
Just as, monk, twenty Sogandhika hells are equal to one Uppala hell;
just as twenty Uppala hells are equal to one Puṇḍarīka hell;
just as twenty Puṇḍarīka hells are equal to one Paduma hell.
“Furthermore, bhikkhu, the bhikkhu Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“For a person who is born,
an axe is born in his mouth,
with which he cuts himself.”
The fool speaks ill-spoken words:
he praises one who deserves blame,
or blames one who is worthy of praise.
He gathers misfortune with his mouth;
through that misfortune, he finds no happiness.
This misfortune is but a trifle.
That loss of wealth at dice— even compared to the loss of all one's possessions together with one's very self—
this alone is the greater evil.
Whoever harbors malice toward the Sugatas will dwell for one hundred thousand *nirabbudas*,
and thirty-six plus five *abbudas*.
One who reviles noble ones goes to hell,
having directed speech and mind toward evil.
Thus ends the first section.
Its summary verse:
Entreaty, respect, Brahmādeva,
Baka the Brahmā, and another view.

2. The Second Chapter:
The Discourse on Sanaṅkumāra.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on the bank of the Sappinī River.
Then Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, at the end of the night, having illuminated the entire bank of the Sappinī with his surpassing radiance, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“The kṣatriya is the best among people who rely on their lineage;”
"Endowed with true knowledge and conduct,
he is the best among gods and humans.
This is what Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra said.
The Teacher gave his approval.
Then Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, thinking, "The Teacher has approved of me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.

2. Second Chapter:
The Discourse on Devadatta.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed.

Then Brahmā Sahampati, having approached Vulture Peak Mountain with a magnificent radiance that illuminated the entire mountain, went to the Blessed One. Having arrived, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Brahmā Sahampati addressed the Blessed One with this verse concerning Devadatta:
"The fruit indeed destroys the plantain tree;
the fruit destroys the bamboo, the fruit destroys the reed."
"Honor kills the base man, just as the fetus destroys the mule.

2. Second Chapter:
The Discourse at Andhakavinda.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Andhakavinda.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air during the pitch-black darkness of night, while a fine rain was falling drop by drop.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, at the end of the night, having illuminated the entire region of Andhakavinda with his surpassing radiance, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Brahmā Sahampati recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Frequent secluded lodgings;
One should wander for the sake of liberation from the fetters.”
If one does not find delight there,
one should dwell in the Saṅgha with self-guarded mind and mindfulness,
wandering from family to family for alms.
Guarded in the senses, prudent, and mindful,
one should frequent remote lodgings,
freed from fear and liberated in the fearless.
Where there are terrifying reptiles,
where lightning flashes and the sky thunders,
on a night of blinding, pitch-black darkness—
There the bhikkhu sat down, his hair standing on end.
For this has indeed been seen by me at last;
it is not mere hearsay.
In a single holy life,
there were a thousand who had overcome death,
and more than five hundred trainees.
Ten times ten makes one hundred;
all these have entered the stream and do not go to the realm of animals.
As for these other people,
my mind considers them to be partakers of merit;
yet I am not even able to calculate [the extent of their merit].
“Shame regarding false speech.

Second Chapter (Dutiyavagga)
The Discourse to Aruṇavata.

Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī … [as above] … The Discourse to Aruṇavata. Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī … [as above] …
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"In the past, monks, there was a king named Aruṇavā.
Now, monks, King Aruṇavā had a royal capital named Aruṇavatī."
“Bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Aruṇavatī.
Now, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Abhibhū and Sambhava, a most auspicious pair.
Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the bhikkhu Abhibhū.”
“Come, brahmin, let us approach a certain world of Brahmā until it is time for our meal.
“Very well, Bhante,” the bhikkhu Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the bhikkhu Abhibhū—just as...
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
even so, having disappeared from the royal capital of Aruṇavatī, they reappeared in that Brahmā world.
Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the bhikkhu Abhibhū:
“May a Dhamma talk occur, brahmin, concerning Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā. “Very well,
Bhante,” the bhikkhu Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and he instructed, exhorted, inspired,
and gladdened Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā with a Dhamma talk.
He incited, inspired, and gladdened them.
Thereupon, monks, Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā were indignant, disparaged him, and complained, saying:
“It is wonderful indeed, sirs! It is marvelous indeed, sirs! How can a disciple teach the Dhamma while the Teacher himself is present?”
Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the bhikkhu Abhibhū:
“Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the followers of Brahmā are indeed complaining, saying:
‘It is wonderful, truly marvelous! How can it be that while the Teacher is present in person, a disciple should teach the Dhamma?’”
"Therefore, brahmin, you should even more thoroughly cause Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā to be moved to spiritual urgency.
"Very well, Bhante," the bhikkhu Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, having given his assent, he taught the Dhamma both with a visible body and with an invisible body.
He taught the Dhamma with his lower half-body visible and his upper half-body invisible;
he also taught the Dhamma with his upper half-body visible and his lower half-body invisible.
Thereupon, monks, Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmās, and the retinue of Brahmās were struck with wonder and amazement, thinking:
“It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir! How great is the psychic power and majesty of this ascetic!
Then the bhikkhu Abhibhū said this to the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“I recall, venerable sir, having spoken such words in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:”
“I am able, friend, standing in the Brahmā world, to make myself heard by voice throughout a thousandfold world-system.
“Now is the time for this, brahmin;
now is the time for this, brahmin—that you, standing in the Brahmā world, should make yourself heard by voice throughout a thousandfold world-system.”
“Yes, Bhante,” the bhikkhu Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Standing in the Brahma-world, he spoke these verses:
“Exert yourselves! Strive!
Devote yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!”
Shake off the army of Death,
as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut—
you who, in this Dhamma and Discipline...
‘He will dwell with diligence;
having abandoned the cycle of birth,
he will make an end of suffering.’”

Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the monk Abhibhū, having inspired a sense of spiritual urgency in the Brahmās, the Brahmā assembly, and the retinue of Brahmās—
just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm, or bend his outstretched arm— they disappeared from that Brahma-world and reappeared in the royal capital of Aruṇavatī.
Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monks:
“Bhikkhus, did you hear the verses being recited by the bhikkhu Abhibhū while he was standing in the Brahmā world? “We heard them, Bhante.
“But how, bhikkhus, did you hear the verses being recited by the bhikkhu Abhibhū while he was standing in the Brahmā world?”
"Thus indeed, Bhante, we heard the verses being recited by the bhikkhu Abhibhū while he was standing in the Brahma-world:
'Exert yourselves! Strive on!
Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!'"
Shake off the army of Death,
as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut—
anyone who, in this Dhamma and Discipline...
‘He will dwell with diligence;
having abandoned the cycle of birth,
he will make an end of suffering.’”
“‘In this way, Bhante, we heard the verses being spoken by the bhikkhu Abhibhū while he was standing in the Brahmā world.
‘Excellent, excellent, bhikkhus!
It is well that you heard the verses being spoken by the bhikkhu Abhibhū while he was standing in the Brahmā world.’”
Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.

Second Chapter (Dutiyavagga)
The Discourse on the Final Nibbāna.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusinārā in the Upavattana sal-tree grove of the Mallas, between a pair of sal trees, at the moment of his final Nibbāna.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Now then, monks, I address you:
‘All conditioned phenomena are subject to decay; strive with diligence.
These were the Tathāgata’s last words.
Then the Blessed One entered the first jhāna. Emerging from the first jhāna, he entered the second jhāna.
Emerging from the second jhāna, he entered the third jhāna. Emerging from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna.
Emerging from the fourth jhāna, he entered the base of infinite space.
Emerging from the base of infinite space, he attained the base of infinite consciousness. Emerging from the base of infinite consciousness, he attained the base of nothingness.
Emerging from the base of nothingness, he attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Emerging from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he attained the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling, he entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Emerging from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the base of nothingness.
Emerging from the base of nothingness, he entered the base of infinite consciousness.
Emerging from the base of infinite consciousness, he entered the base of infinite space. Emerging from the base of infinite space...
Emerging from that, he entered the fourth jhāna. Emerging from the fourth jhāna, he entered the third jhāna.

Emerging from the third jhāna, he entered the second jhāna. Emerging from the second jhāna, he entered the first jhāna. Emerging from the first jhāna, he entered the second jhāna. Emerging from the second...
Emerging from that jhāna, he entered the third jhāna. Emerging from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna.
Emerging from the fourth jhāna, immediately thereafter, the Blessed One attained final nibbāna.
When the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, at the moment of his passing, Brahmā Sahampati recited this verse:
“All beings in the world will eventually lay down their physical frame,
wherever such a Teacher as this [has appeared].”
The peerless person in the world,
the Tathāgata who has attained the powers,
the Perfectly Enlightened One, has attained final Nibbāna.”
When the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, immediately upon his passing, Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke this verse:
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned things,
subject to arising and passing away;”
“Having arisen, they cease;
their subsiding is blissful.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, immediately upon his passing, the Venerable Ānanda recited this verse:
“Then there was that which was terrifying,
then there was that which made the hair stand on end;
[yet you remain] endowed with the excellence of all forms.”
“When the Fully Awakened One has attained final Nibbāna.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, immediately upon his passing, the Venerable Anuruddha spoke these verses:
“I have neither in-breath nor out-breath;”
For the one of such a nature whose mind is steadfast,
the seer who has attained peace, being free from passion, has entered final nibbāna.
With a mind undaunted,
he endured the sensation;
like the extinguishing of a lamp, [he attained Nibbāna].
“...there was liberation of the mind.

Its summary verse:
